ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Suppose the orbit of the quantum satellite is in the equatorial plane, as shown in Figure 1. It is known that the orbital radius of the quantum satellite is m times the Earth's radius, and the orbital radius of the geostationary satellite is n times the Earth's radius. ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the Earth is located at the center and is labeled “Earth”; there is a point P at the equatorial position on the Earth's surface. Outside the Earth there are two concentric circular orbits; the inner orbit is labeled “quantum satellite,” and the outer orbit is labeled “geostationary satellite,” indicating that both the quantum satellite and the geostationary satellite move in circular motion around the Earth, and point P moves on the equator with the Earth's rotation. Then reason: Let the Earth's radius be R, the Earth's mass be M, and the gravitational constant be G. The problem states that the orbital radius of the quantum satellite is r_q=mR, and the orbital radius of the geostationary satellite is r_g=nR. When the quantum satellite moves in circular motion, the universal gravitational force provides the centripetal force: GMm_s/r_q^2=m_s v_q^2/r_q, so v_q=\sqrt{GM/r_q}=\sqrt{GM/(mR)}. The geostationary satellite has the same angular velocity as the Earth's rotation. For the geostationary satellite in an orbit with radius r_g=nR, there is \omega_E=\sqrt{GM/r_g^3}=\sqrt{GM/(nR)^3}. Point P is on the surface of the Earth's equator, and its linear velocity as it follows the Earth's rotation is v_P=\omega_E R=R\sqrt{GM/(nR)^3}=\sqrt{GM/(n^3R)}. Therefore, the ratio of the speed of the quantum satellite to that of point P is v_q/v_P=\sqrt{GM/(mR)} / \sqrt{GM/(n^3R)}=\sqrt{n^3/m}.
